'''''Murraya paniculata''''', commonly known as '''orange jasmine''', '''orange jessamine''', '''china box''', '''cosmetic barktree''', or '''mock orange''',<ref name="RFK" /> is a species of shrub or small tree in the family [[Rutaceae]] and is [[Indigenous (ecology)|native]] to South Asia, Southeast Asia and Australia. It has smooth bark, [[Pinnation|pinnate]] leaves with up to seven egg-shaped to elliptical leaflets, fragrant white or cream-coloured flowers and oval, orange-red berries containing hairy seeds.

==Description==
''Murraya paniculata'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|7|m}} but often flowers and forms fruit as a shrub, and has smooth pale to whitish bark. It has pinnate leaves up to {{cvt|17|cm}} long with up to seven egg-shaped to elliptical or [[rhombus]]-shaped. The leaflets are glossy green and [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]], {{cvt|2.5–10|cm|0}} long and {{cvt|12–50|mm|1}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiolule]] {{cvt|2–6|mm|2}} long.{{R|RFK|FOA|efl|WEEDS}}

The flowers are fragrant and are arranged in loose groups, each flower on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] about {{cvt|1.5|mm|2}} long. There are five (sometimes four) [[sepal]]s about {{cvt|1|mm|2}} long and five (sometimes four) white or cream-coloured petals {{cvt|13–18|mm|1}} long. and the fruit is an oval, glabrous, orange-red berry {{cvt|12–14|mm|2}} long containing densely hairy seeds.{{R|RFK|FOA|efl|WEEDS}} 

===Phenology===
Flowering occurs from June to March in Australia, and the fruit ripen between January and October.{{R|FOA|COOPER2}} In the northern hemisphere flowering occurs from April to October and fruit ripen from April to February.{{R|FOC}}

==Taxonomy==
This species was first described and illustrated by [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius]] in the latter half of the 17th century during his time in what was then known as the [[Dutch East Indies]], and published posthumously in 1747.{{R|RUMPH}} However the first [[Species description|formal description]] was produced in 1767 by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] who gave it the name ''Chalcas paniculata'' and published it in his book ''[[Mantissa Plantarum]]'', which is an appendix to the [[12th edition of Systema Naturae|12th edition]] of his earlier work [[Systema Naturae]].{{R|LINNAEUS|APNI1}} In 1820 the Scottish botanist [[William Jack (botanist)|William Jack]] changed the name to ''Murraya paniculata'' in his book ''Descriptions of Malayan Plants [Malayan Miscellanies]''.{{R|APNI|JACK}}

==Distribution and habitat==
''Murraya paniculata'' grows in rainforest, often as an [[Understory|understorey]] shrub in vine thickets, including behind beaches. It is native to [[South Asia|South]] and [[Southeast Asia]], China and [[Australasia]], while the distribution area extends from Pakistan via India, Sri Lanka and southern China to Taiwan, the Philippines, where it is called ''kamuníng'',<ref name="Philippine Medicinal Plants">{{cite web |title=''Kamuning'' |url=http://www.stuartxchange.org/Kamuning.html |publisher=Stuartxchange |accessdate=21 November 2021 |archive-date=20 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211120162101/http://www.stuartxchange.org/Kamuning.html |url-status=live }}</ref> the [[Ryūkyū Islands]] and the [[Mariana Islands]], to the south via Malaysia and Indonesia to New Guinea and parts of Australia.<ref name="FOA" /><ref name="POWO"/> In Australia, it is native to the [[Kimberley, Western Australia|Kimberley]] region of [[Western Australia]], northern parts of the [[Northern Territory]], and parts of [[Queensland]].<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Murraya paniculata''|id=4491}}</ref><ref name="efloraNT">{{cite web |title=''Murraya paniculata'' |url=http://eflora.nt.gov.au/factsheet?id=5305 |publisher=Northern Territory Government |accessdate=29 July 2020}}</ref> The species has been naturalised in other places, sometimes becoming an invasive weed, including on many Pacific islands.{{R|PIER}} In Queensland, it is regarded as different from the cultivated form ''Murraya paniculata'' 'Exotica', which is regarded as one of the most invasive plant species in southeast Queensland.<ref name="WEEDS" />

==Cultivation==
''Murraya paniculata'' is cultivated as an ornamental tree or hedge because of its hardiness, wide range of soil tolerance (''M. paniculata'' may grow in [[alkaline]], clayey, sandy, [[acid]]ic and [[loam]]y soils), and is suitable for larger hedges. The plant flowers throughout the year and produces small, fragrant flower clusters which attract bees, while the fruits attract small [[frugivore|frugivorous]] birds.<ref name="efl" />

===Propagation===
The orange jessamine is sexually [[Plant propagation|propagated]] by its seeds. The fruits are eaten by birds, which then pass the seeds out in their [[feces]]. It may also be asexually propagated by softwood cuttings.<ref name="efl" />

==Ecology==
This species is one of the preferred hosts of the citrus pest ''[[Diaphorina citri]]'', the citrus psyllid, which is the vector for the [[Citrus greening disease]].{{R|PIER|HALBERT}}

===Diseases===
''M. paniculata'' is vulnerable to soil [[nematode]]s, scales, [[sooty mold]] and [[whitefly|whiteflies]].<ref name="efl" />
